html:
Laterite stone walls up to six metres high near Loropeni in southwestern Burkina Faso, at least a thousand years old, the best preserved of about a hundred such enclosures in the region.

They are linked to the trade in gold from the nearby Lobi fields, which went north on the trans-Saharan trade, and the site flourished from the 14th to the 17th centuries. Who built the walls, and why, is still uncertain; local peoples such as the Koulango and Lohron have traditions about them. UNESCO made them Burkina Faso's first World Heritage Site in 2009. They are much older than the Mossi kingdoms to the north. See also Ghana and the gold trade.
sum: Laterite stone walls up to six metres high near Loropeni in southwestern Burkina Faso, at least a thousand years old, the best preserved of about a hundred such enclosures in the region.
